```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(repair)
stopifnot(requireNamespace("nlme", quietly = TRUE))
```

## Fit a relationship between two processes

Each MLM estimates a person's random coefficients from repeated
observations. Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression
(REPAIR) fits a structural regression using their likelihood-only
predictions and sampling-error covariance. For example, one process's slope can
predict another process's slope, adjusting for the first process's intercept.
The two MLMs may use different occasions and grouping column names.
Their ID values must identify the same units; REPAIR cannot infer an ID crosswalk.

This example uses packaged synthetic observations and frozen reference results
from the paper's simulation functions. It reproduces the dual-process computation,
not the published Monte Carlo tables. Ordinary use supplies your own fitted
models and unit-level data; no fixture is needed.

```{r models}
reference <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "multimodel-workflow-reference.rds",
                               package = "repair"))
case <- reference$cases$independent
models <- list(
  growth = nlme::lme(y ~ z, random = ~ z | id, data = case$a),
  response = nlme::lme(q ~ w, random = ~ w | subject, data = case$b)
)
repair_effects(models)
structural <- re("w", "response") ~
  re("(Intercept)", "growth") + re("z", "growth")
fit <- repair(structural, models, case$people, id = "person",
              cross_model_error = "independent")
summary(fit)
```

`re("z", "growth")` selects the growth model's random slope for `z`; it is a
deviation from its fixed slope. `repair_effects()` lists available scalar names.
`repair_data()` performs the same assembly as `repair()` without fitting the
structural regression, allowing you to inspect predictions and error inputs first.

## Choose a prediction-error assumption

The `cross_model_error` argument is required when the formula references multiple
models. It is not required merely because an unused model is in the supplied list.

- `"independent"` sets all **between-model prediction-error covariances** to zero.
  It retains all within-model covariances, including intercept/slope covariance.
- A list of named covariance blocks supplies the between-model covariances.
  Every unordered pair of referenced models must have a block, even if it is zero.
- `NULL`, the default, is accepted only for a single referenced model.

Correlated latent slopes do not necessarily have correlated prediction errors.
Conversely, separate MLM fits do not establish independent errors.
Shared occasion-level disturbances or overlapping measurements can correlate the
errors. Choose the policy from the measurement design and a defensible covariance
model. The package does not estimate that covariance from separate fitted models.

### Where do these covariances come from?

The target is the covariance of the **estimation errors in the likelihood-only
predictions**, conditional on fitted measurement parameters. It is different from
the covariance between people's true intercepts/slopes. Correlating extracted
slopes across people mixes true between-person variation with prediction error;
it does not estimate the needed error covariance.

Start with the measurement design:

| Design or evidence | Practical action |
|:--|:--|
| Defensible independent measurement errors, conditional on each process's target effects | Use `"independent"`, and state why. Sharing people alone does not contradict this assumption. |
| Paired occasions with plausible shared noise | Specify an observation-level cross-error model and propagate it with `repair_cross_covariance()`. Examine a range of justified assumptions with `repair_sensitivity()`. |
| Calibration data or a jointly fitted multivariate measurement model | Obtain compatible observation error covariances from that source, separating residual/nuisance covariance from target random-effect covariance. Supply the observation blocks or externally propagated prediction blocks. |
| Insufficient evidence to choose one covariance | Report sensitivity over a scientifically plausible range. The package cannot turn unidentified assumptions into empirical estimates. |

Separate fits do not demonstrate independent errors. Different occasions do not
guarantee independence either: persistent or serially correlated disturbances
can bridge occasions. Conversely, correlated latent processes do not by
themselves require nonzero cross-error blocks. The relevant assumption concerns
the noise remaining after the target random coefficients are separated out.

Ordinary mixed-model residual correlations are not an automatic solution.
For example, `nlme::residuals()` depends on the chosen grouping level and residual
type; conditional residuals also reflect estimation and shrinkage of random
effects. They are not interchangeable with observation errors or prediction
errors. See the [nlme residual documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/nlme/html/residuals.lme.html).
A joint multivariate measurement model can distinguish residual correlations from
cross-process random-effect correlations; the
[brms multivariate guide](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_multivariate.html)
illustrates that distinction. REPAIR does not directly accept brms fits: an
external covariance source must be compatible with the supported marginal fits,
measurement scales, IDs, occasions, and effective nuisance covariance.

Each model must select one target grouping factor. lmer models can also have
nuisance groups contained within each target person; see `vignette("nested-nuisance")`.
Multiple models do not relax the independent-person assumption: shared nuisance
groups remain rejected because their cross-person error covariance cannot enter
this estimator. Models may mix supported lmer and single-group lme backends.

## Supply nonzero cross-model covariance

Each block has `models = c("a", "b")` and a numeric `covariance` array with
three dimensions: selected coefficient names from a, selected coefficient names
from b, and unit IDs. All dimensions must be named. These are covariances in
**prediction units**, not correlations, BLUP posterior covariances, or raw residual
covariances. Names come from `repair_effects()` and the unit-level ID column.

For linear prediction extraction operators L_a and L_b, an externally justified residual
cross-covariance R_ab gives prediction covariance L_a R_ab L_b-transpose. Deriving
R_ab and matching the repeated observations is an analyst responsibility. This
fixture uses a known residual correlation of 0.25 and fitted marginal residual
scales; its generator performs that propagation independently of this package.

```{r supplied}
correlated <- reference$cases$supplied
models2 <- list(
  growth = nlme::lme(y ~ z, random = ~ z | id, data = correlated$a),
  response = nlme::lme(q ~ w, random = ~ w | subject, data = correlated$b)
)
# Prepared externally by the fixture generator, not inferred from the two fits.
score_cross_covariance <- correlated$cross_model_error[[1]]$covariance
dim(score_cross_covariance)  # 2 growth coefficients x 1 response coefficient x 70 IDs
dimnames(score_cross_covariance)[1:2]
blocks <- list(list(models = c("growth", "response"),
                    covariance = score_cross_covariance))
fit2 <- repair(structural, models2, correlated$people, "person",
               cross_model_error = blocks)
head(fit2@analysis_data@err_xy)
summary(fit2)$cross_model_error$policy
```

Term names must exactly cover the coefficients selected by the formula, not
necessarily every coefficient in the fitted model. Every retained person must
have a block entry; extra IDs are permitted. Row, column, ID, model-list, and
block ordering do not matter. Reversing a pair requires transposing its first
two array dimensions. Supply a pair only once; REPAIR supplies its transpose.
Within-model error blocks are computed by the scorer and cannot be overridden.
The complete assembled covariance must be positive semidefinite for each person;
checking pairs separately would be insufficient for three or more models.

The policy and original supplied blocks remain in
`fit@analysis_data@diagnostics$cross_model_error` and `summary(fit)$cross_model_error`.
The estimator's final aligned inputs are `@err_x`, `@err_y`, and `@err_xy`.
Standard errors condition on the MLM fits and supplied covariance; they
do not propagate uncertainty in estimating either.

## Propagate observation covariance with a helper

`repair_cross_covariance()` computes the extraction operators from the fitted
models and propagates supplied observation error assumptions:

\[
L_{a,i} = (Z_{a,i}^{\mathsf T}R_{a,i}^{-1}Z_{a,i})^{-1}
           Z_{a,i}^{\mathsf T}R_{a,i}^{-1}, \qquad
\Omega_{ab,i} = L_{a,i}R_{ab,i}L_{b,i}^{\mathsf T}.
\]

Here R_a and R_b are the fitted effective error covariances used by the scorer,
including contained nuisance random effects when present; they exclude the target
random effects. R_ab describes covariance between those effective observation
errors. Only the formula-selected coefficients are returned. The helper does
not refit a joint model or estimate R_ab.

### Matched occasions under an assumed iid correlation

For two models with homoscedastic iid errors and no nuisance random groups, the
`rho` shortcut assumes correlation rho at matching occasions for the same person,
and zero covariance at all other occasion pairs. This fixture has known matching
time scales: z = time / 4 and w = 0.5 + time / 5. Its generating rho = 0.25 is
known only because the data are synthetic; this is not an empirical estimate.

```{r propagate-iid}
# Values are occasion keys, names identify original observation rows.
# Real data should use recorded visit/occasion identifiers, on a common scale.
keys <- list(
  growth = setNames(as.character(round(4 * correlated$a$z)), rownames(correlated$a)),
  response = setNames(as.character(round(5 * (correlated$b$w - .5))),
                      rownames(correlated$b))
)
propagated <- repair_cross_covariance(structural, models2, keys,
  rho = .25, ids = correlated$people$person)
fit_propagated <- repair(structural, models2, correlated$people, "person",
                         cross_model_error = propagated)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(coef(fit_propagated), coef(fit2), tolerance = 1e-12)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(vcov(fit_propagated), vcov(fit2), tolerance = 1e-12)))
```

Keys are matched to **effective fitted row names**, so original input order,
subsetting and omitted rows do not silently change alignment. Supply unique,
nonempty occasion keys within each person and model; they can repeat between
people. Equal keys identify equal occasions across models. Preserve the original
row names in the key vectors. The helper never pairs by row position or nearest
time. Unmatched occasions have zero cross-covariance under this shortcut, an
assumption that needs justification for your design. The shortcut rejects
correlated or heterogeneous marginal errors; a plausible scalar rho alone is
insufficient to specify a joint covariance for those models.

### Explicit observation blocks

For more general errors, supply a matrix R_ab for every requested person and
every unordered pair of referenced models. Matrix row and column names identify
effective occasion keys in the two models; these matrices may be rectangular.
The following explicitly constructs the same iid assumption for illustration:

```{r propagate-explicit}
observation_covariance <- lapply(correlated$people$person, function(person) {
  a <- keys$growth[rownames(correlated$a)[correlated$a$id == person]]
  b <- keys$response[rownames(correlated$b)[correlated$b$subject == person]]
  rab <- outer(unname(a), unname(b), `==`) * .25 *
    sigma(models2$growth) * sigma(models2$response)
  dimnames(rab) <- list(a, b)
  rab
})
names(observation_covariance) <- correlated$people$person
explicit <- repair_cross_covariance(structural, models2, keys,
  residual_cross_covariance = list(list(models = c("growth", "response"),
    covariance = observation_covariance)), ids = correlated$people$person)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(explicit, propagated, tolerance = 1e-12)))
```

In a real analysis, replace those matrices with a scientifically justified joint
error model or compatible external calibration. Their entries are observation
covariances, not correlations. For nested nuisance groups, include any cross-model
nuisance covariance in addition to residual covariance. Automatic estimation from
paired residuals would need its own statistical method and validation and is
outside this workflow.

The helper checks the **complete joint observation covariance** using fitted
within-model blocks, then checks the propagated selected-effect covariance.
With three or more models, valid pairs need not form a valid joint covariance.
It rejects invalid inputs rather than projecting them to a nearby matrix.
The fitted marginal blocks are preserved. Incompatible external estimates must
be reconciled through the measurement model, not silently modified here.

## Examine sensitivity to the cross-error assumption

Choose a range from substantive knowledge of the measurement errors, calibration,
or external studies. The values below are illustrative and not a recommended
universal range. A sensitivity grid is not a confidence interval for rho, and
choosing the scenario with the preferred structural result would undermine its
purpose. Keep other fitting choices and the analysis scope fixed.

```{r sensitivity}
rhos <- c(-.5, 0, .25, .5)
scenario_names <- paste0("rho=", rhos)
constructed <- setNames(vector("list", length(rhos)), scenario_names)
construction <- data.frame(scenario = scenario_names, rho = rhos,
                           status = "ok", message = "")
for (j in seq_along(rhos)) {
  # Preserve construction failures as well as downstream fitting failures.
  constructed[j] <- list(tryCatch(
    repair_cross_covariance(structural, models2, keys, rho = rhos[j],
                             ids = correlated$people$person),
    error = function(e) {
      construction$status[j] <<- "error"
      construction$message[j] <<- conditionMessage(e)
      NULL
    }))
}
construction
scenarios <- c(list(independent = "independent"),
               constructed[construction$status == "ok"])
sensitivity <- repair_sensitivity(structural, models2, correlated$people,
  "person", scenarios = scenarios, regularization = "step_up")
sensitivity$scenarios  # status, warnings, selected alphas, fallback flags
sensitivity$coefficients[, c("scenario", "term", "estimate", "std.error",
                             "conf.low", "conf.high")]
# Inspect full diagnostics for a particular assumption.
repair_diagnostics(sensitivity$fits[["rho=0.25"]], table = "conditioning")
stopifnot(identical(sensitivity$fits$independent@struc_fit,
                    sensitivity$fits[["rho=0"]]@struc_fit))
```

The models are reused across scenarios; `repair_mlm()` specifications, if
supplied, are fitted once for the whole sensitivity call. Each scenario uses the
existing estimator and reselects step-up alphas when requested. Scenario-specific
invalid covariance inputs have status `"error"`, numerical structural failures
have status `"failed"`, and neither produces coefficient rows. A usable
minimum-alpha fallback remains `"ok"` with explicit fallback flags. Shared input
errors stop the call. Warnings during each scenario are saved in its summary.
Construction failures occur before `repair_sensitivity()`, so keep the
`construction` table alongside its outputs, as above.

Report the assumptions, admissible range, rejected or failed scenarios, and how
the estimates, SEs, intervals, and regularization change. Intervals remain
conditional on each assumed covariance and the fitted marginal model parameters.
They do not average over scenarios or include uncertainty in an estimated error
correlation. The existing whole-unit bootstrap supports a single measurement
model; this sensitivity workflow does not add a multiple-model bootstrap or
propagate uncertainty in externally estimated cross-model parameters.

## Check matching and exclusions

The unit-level data frame defines the scope and output order. Each model's
predictions are matched to it by ID. By default an absent ID, failed prediction, or
missing/nonfinite observed structural variable stops assembly. With
`na_action = "omit"`, REPAIR warns and records the ID and all applicable reasons,
including the responsible model names. It never matches by row position.
Invalid covariance specifications are errors even with omission enabled.

```{r diagnostics}
a <- fit@analysis_data
a@diagnostics$excluded
lapply(a@diagnostics$mlm_models, function(x) x$unused_prediction_ids)
names(a@predictions)  # named by model for multiple-model analyses
head(a@predictions$growth@predictions$id)
```

For single-model analyses, `@predictions` remains the original prediction object.
`@diagnostics$mlm_models` is always a named list, giving a consistent
way to inspect grouping names, backend, unused IDs, singularity, and fit messages.

## Reproduce coefficients, standard errors, and intervals

The frozen expectations were produced without loading `repair`, using the paper's
production prediction extraction helper, full M-MOM implementation, primary dual-process
estimator, and independent algebra audit. Tests refit both MLMs
from observations and compare both R and C++ computation backends.

```{r reproduce}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(fit)), case$coefficients$estimate,
                          tolerance = 1e-5)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(vcov(fit)), unname(case$vcov),
                          tolerance = 1e-5)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(confint(fit)),
  unname(as.matrix(case$coefficients[, c("ci_low", "ci_high")])), tolerance = 1e-5)))
# The simulation reports a standardized focal slope using a population SD ratio.
# This known generating ratio is NOT the SD ratio of noisy estimated predictions.
focal <- tail(fit@struc_fit@coefficients, 1)[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_low", "ci_high")]
rownames(focal) <- NULL
reported <- focal * case$reporting_scale
reported
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(reported, case$reported_focal, tolerance = 1e-5)))
```

The package estimates on the input scale. The paper's dual-process reporting
scale is population predictor-slope SD divided by population outcome-slope SD.
Apply the same positive factor to the focal estimate, SE, and interval endpoints.
For empirical analyses, choose and disclose a justified reporting scale;
estimated scale uncertainty is not included by multiplying the output.

Fixture provenance records source commit and hashes, R/nlme versions, and the
modified preliminary moment and final covariance bread. The source repository's
`dev/generate_multimodel_fixtures.R` and `dev/multimodel-validation.md` document
the generation and validation workflow.
